newsitem.title: USA: Crew, controller cited in Connecticut air accident.
newsitem.headline: Crew, controller cited in Connecticut air accident.

text.p: U.S. safety officials Wednesday blamed both the crew of an American Airlines MD-83 and ground control for the plane's tree-clipping approach to Bradley airport, near Hartford, Conn. on Nov. 12, 1995.
One of the 77 people aboard was injured when the plane, on a flight from Chicago, landed on grassy, even terrain just short of the runway.
Making the approch in stormy weather, the plane clipped branches for some 250 feet before bouncing to a stop. It sustained substantial damage.

The National Transportation Safety Board said the significant atmospheric change caused by the storm would have affected the plane's altimeter setting, making it difficult for the crew to judge altitude.

"Because the flight crew knew that atmospheric pressure was falling rapidly, they should have requested a current altimeter setting from BDL (Bradley airport) approach controller when one was not given, as required, upon initial radio contact." the board said.
It added that if the crew had gotten a new altimeter reading, it likely would have brought the plane 40 feet higher, giving the craft enough clearance to miss the trees.

The board's recommendations to the Federal Aviation Adminsistration included a tightening of regulations for instrument approaches and changes in approach procedures at Bradley because of the region's terrain.
